To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
urban vegetation may contribute significantly to ozone formation in urban areas during heat waves.
the contribution of vegetation to ozone formation during heat wave periods can increase significantly and that urban greening programs need to consider these effects.
the heat wave in summer 2006 increased the emissions of VOCs from urban vegetation and the contribution of these emissions to ozone formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the feedbacks between the urban system and vegetation and the potential of urban greening to reduce ozone formation in the urban atmosphere.
the feedbacks between vegetation, air quality, and climate change.
how the urban system responds to extreme events, such as heat waves, and what the implications of this response are for urban air quality and climate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
urban greening programs may have a negative effect on air quality during heat waves.

urban greening programs may be effective to reduce summer temperatures and storm water control, but the potential for emissions of VOCs from urban vegetation should be taken into account to prevent negative impacts on urban air quality.
urban greening programs should be accompanied by an assessment of the impact of the program on air quality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
urban greening programs need to take into account the coupling between urban and sub urban vegetation and the atmosphere, as well as the feedbacks between the two.
the vegetation in urban areas may contribute to the ozone formation and thus to the urban air pollution, especially in the summer months.
the vegetation in cities can be a source of ozone precursors under extreme weather conditions and thus should be considered when planning urban greening projects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the vegetation should be considered in urban air quality management.
urban greening programs should take into consideration how vegetation responds to elevated temperature.
the benefits of urban greening may be counterbalanced by increased emissions of biogenic VOCs.
